stories.title: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
stories.summary: Data centers are deeply unpopular. But what if we called them something else?

sources.name: TechCrunch AI
sources.title: OpenAI might rebrand its data centers as ‘AI compute campuses’
sources.text: Data centers are deeply unpopular . But what if we called them something else? Axios reports that OpenAI is preparing a “PR blitz” for after the midterm elections on Tuesday, as Democrats seem likely to win back the House of Representatives, and possibly the Senate, too . The company’s chief global affairs officer Chris Lehane told Axios that the midterms will be “a bit of a movie trailer for what you’re going to see in 2028,” when he expects AI to be “ the issue” in the presidential election. So OpenAI is to influence the AI debate moving forward, with Lehane discussing several proposals, including the development of AI “speed limits” ; finding ways to help people see AI as empowering them in their daily lives; pushing the U.S. to take a role in developing global standards; and yes — rebranding data centers as “AI compute campuses.” Lehane also described the conversation around data centers (a debate that has pushed Amazon and Microsoft to say they will no longer use NDAs in their negotiations with local governments ) as “good and healthy.” “Communities should hold companies responsible and accountable so they really and truly get a transformative benefit from these projects,” he said. sources.name: TechRadar
sources.title: Russia wants to camouflage its data centers to stop them being bombed — and it might even move them underground for protection
sources.text: Ukraine’s increasing targeting of Russian data infrastructure has resulted in Moscow considering new defensive measures against drone strikes. The Digital Development Ministry has proposed a list of countermeasures and precautions against attack, ranging from jamming hardware and camouflage to building subterranean data centers. With experts warning that a data center outage could leave a facility value wiped by up to 87%, Russia is taking steps to protect is cloud and AI facilities. But such action could increase costs for each facility by around 10%. Pushing up the potential cost of future data centers, safety measures include protection against shockwaves for servers, power supplies, and cooling systems. Throughout 2026, Ukraine has stepped up its retaliatory strikes against Russian industrial assets, most recently with five data centers targeted in October. Among these was country’s largest facility, based in ‌Balakovo and owned by Sberbank. Others targeted include three data centers owned by Yandex. At the time, Sberbank First Deputy CEO Alexander Vedyakhin told reporters that "We confirm that the data processing center was attacked. At the same time, all of Sberbank's systems and services are operating normally and without disruption." The Digital Development Ministry recommendations were seen by Russian publication Kommersant , which noted that the ministry had confirmed “The development of recommendations has been completed, the document [...] sent to the relevant organizations.” Sign up to the TechRadar Pro newsletter to get all the top news, opinion, features and guidance your business needs to succeed! It appears that the document was initially circulated on October 21 2026, possibly in response to the ‌Balakovo data center strike, and certainly as a reaction to the wider concerns. Kommersant indicates that Russian businesses and citizens are concerned about Ukraine’s targeting of internet infrastructure. Not all data centers are considered to be equal within the plans, which divide the facilities into three categories. K1 indicates strategic targets, K2 is economic targets, while K3 is a signifier of a corporate site. While the exact strategies for each category is unknown, it seems likely that the K1 targets would be subjected to the largest defensive measures. While it might be costly to install shockwave protection, anti-drone nets and signal jammers are likely more affordable elements. The cost of installing shelters and other protections is preferable to the alternative, according to Roman Chustuzian, senior investment director of KAMA FLOW, who told Kommersant: “Even if shelters, grids, sensors and duplication of connections add 5-10% to the cost of the object, it is not comparable with the loss of 87% of its cost and months of downtime.” Follow TechRadar on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our expert news, reviews, and opinion in your feeds. He has contributed to TechRadar since 2017 and has been published in Computer Weekly, Linux Format, ComputerActive, and other publications. stories.title: OpenAI appoints Dan Driscoll as Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization
stories.summary: OpenAI appoints Dan Driscoll to advise on responsible AI for national security modernization, cyber resilience, and collaboration with U.S. allies.

sources.name: OpenAI
sources.title: OpenAI appoints Dan Driscoll as Senior Counselor for National Security Modernization

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: OpenAI hires former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll for national security role
sources.text: OpenAI has hired former U.S. Army Secretary Dan Driscoll as senior counselor for national security modernization, a newly created role at the company . Driscoll will focus on how artificial intelligence can be used to strengthen U.S. national security and cybersecurity, OpenAI said, while his updated LinkedIn profile also lists his new position. He will work with OpenAI's senior leadership and external partners, with a particular focus on helping U.S. allies adopt advanced AI responsibly. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman said the U.S. has "an extraordinary opportunity to work with other countries to spread the adoption of democratic AI," and that Driscoll's appointment would help strengthen American leadership in the technology. "National security requirements are changing faster than at any time in the past fifty years," Driscoll said. He added that AI could help reduce paperwork, process information and deliver answers more quickly to those working in national security. The appointment comes after Driscoll stepped down as Army secretary earlier this year after months of reported tensions with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. An Iraq war veteran, Driscoll pushed efforts to modernize the U.S. military, including expanding access to drone and counter-drone technologies among U.S. allies, according to a previous U.S. Army announcement. Driscoll also met with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv in November 2025 to discuss a U.S.-proposed peace plan aimed at ending the war with Russia, according to a statement from the Presidential Office of Ukraine. At OpenAI, Driscoll will work with government officials, industry leaders, academic institutions and allied organizations to advance what the company calls "democratic AI." He will also help internal teams understand the operational needs of national security institutions, building on OpenAI's efforts to strengthen cyber resilience and protect essential services through its Daybreak program .

stories.title: Brookfield plans for a $27 billion AI data center at UK power station
stories.summary: Europe is scrambling to develop infrastructure to support the rollout of AI amid high energy and land costs.

sources.name: CNBC Technology
sources.title: Brookfield plans for a $27 billion AI data center at UK power station
sources.text: Brookfield is targeting a massive artificial intelligence data center in the north of England, as Europe scrambles to develop infrastructure to support the rollout of AI amid high energy and land costs. Energy company Drax Group said Tuesday it has signed an agreement with Brookfield and the asset manager's neocloud platform Radiant to jointly develop an AI data center on the Drax Power Station estate in North Yorkshire. London-listed shares of Drax were up 8.8% in early morning trading. The project is initially targeting up to 100 megawatts of capacity to be operational from the first quarter of 2028, with an additional 500 MW of capacity to be brought online between 2028 and 2031. It is then looking to secure more than 1 gigawatt of capacity at the site by an unspecified date. Brookfield estimates total investment, including semiconductors, could exceed £20 billion ($26.8 billion), with an initial £2.5 billion investment in phase 1. "This is a unique opportunity for the UK's AI ecosystem to build at scale," Radiant CEO Mahdi Yahya said in a statement. "By designing, building and operating from the UK, it will give British researchers, startups and enterprises access to frontier compute at home." The first phase of Brookfield's project in North Yorkshire will use power from the grid and target commercial customers from early 2028. The initial phase is subject to planning, regulatory and network approvals from the government and relevant agencies, alongside securing a tenant for the project, Drax said in a statement said. The company added that final investment decisions are yet to be made. While the U.S. has surged ahead on developing the huge data centers needed to power AI, Europe has been slower to break ground on the facilities. The U.K. in particular has struggled with high energy costs and challenges with long waiting times for businesses to connect to the grid. In October, it was reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid. An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC at the time that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site." Unlike the U.K., the Nordics benefit from abundant power and available land. Countries in the region, like Finland, have seen major commitments to develop AI data centers this year. In September, Google said it would invest at least 13 billion euros ($15.1 billion) into AI infrastructure in the country, marking the tech giant's largest single investment in Europe.

sources.name: The Verge AI
sources.title: OpenAI pitches data center power plants as a way to protect nearby areas
sources.text: As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters. As public opinion has soured on data centers, it’s selling ‘AI campuses’ as protectors, instead of noisy polluters. In an announcement on Monday , OpenAI says it will pilot its “Grid Protectors Program” at an upcoming data center in Effingham County, Georgia, where the company promises to free up to 1,000 megawatts of power during extreme weather or emergencies, enough to power air conditioners in around 700,000 homes. The announcement comes as opposition to data centers spreads across the US, in response to massive projects that have begun development and construction, frequently with little or no input from local residents. In Utah, residents protested after Box Elder County commissioners signed off on a data center expected to consume more than double the state’s peak electricity demand in 2025, and spread hot air in the desert valley surrounding the data center. Now OpenAI’s approach is to pitch the construction of power plants that feed the electricity required by the new AI data centers it’s building as “a resource that utilities can call on when communities need it most.” Several states like Tennessee, Florida, Oklahoma, Oregon, and others have enacted laws that say they will prevent AI companies from passing energy costs on to residents, in addition to moratoriums and other restrictions. This is besides the environmental impacts, as a recent study by the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC) said that powering proposed Texas data center projects could undo decades of air quality gains over just five years. OpenAI, which has switched to calling its AI data centers “compute campuses” in an effort to separate from their poor public reputation , claims it helps reduce costs for customers by operating year-round: “Electricity demand also rises and falls with the seasons, with different regions facing their biggest peaks at different times,” OpenAI’s announcement says. “Our compute campuses need power year-round. With the right agreements, that steady demand can help spread the grid’s fixed costs across more electricity sales, while flexibility lets us reduce demand when the system is busiest.” OpenAI says it’s going to continue working with policymakers and utility services to make “arrangements for our future campus to reduce electricity demand when the grid is under strain.” Along with its data center in Georgia, OpenAI is also partnering with Oracle and SoftBank to build its “Stargate” data centers across the US, including in Shackelford County, Texas; Doña Ana County, New Mexico; and Milam County, Texas.
